questions.question: Do you use a gas burner purely out of necessity? I know you also use the wok on your induction.

hybrid.answer:
No, it isn't just necessity. I prefer a small portable butane burner for wok cooking, even when I had a full gas range at home [1]. I do also use my wok on induction, and it works fine for good stir-frying, but you can't get wok flavor out of it [2].

**Why I prefer the portable burner**
- A butane burner tops out around 15,000 BTU, but its flame is concentrated and points up at the center, so it's much more effective than a Western range [1].
- A Western range spreads heat out evenly for a big skillet. With a wok, a lot of that energy flows up the sides and heats the air instead of the metal in the center [3].
- Heat matters, but BTU alone isn't the measure. What matters more is where the heat is focused [4].
- Look for a portable burner around 12,500 BTU or higher. I'd say that works better than a standard Western home burner, even one with a higher rating [5].

**Why gas matters for flavor**
- Dishes like fried rice or fried noodles depend on the smoky wok flavor, and you can't really get that on induction unless you use a blowtorch [6].
- The most important element of that flavor is the gas flame leaping into the wok and igniting the aerosolized oil coming off the food. That's difficult on induction because there's no live flame [7].

**On induction**
- Most dishes that don't need wok flavor cook very easily on induction [8].
- Toss less and use your spatula more, because the wok often isn't in contact with the burner while you toss [9].

**Using it indoors**
- You can put a portable butane burner on an electric or induction cooktop under your hood so the smoke vents out [10].

questions.question: How often do you oil your wooden cutting boards and utensils?

hybrid.answer:
I oil them as needed, not on a fixed schedule. For the cutting board that's maybe a few times a year, and I oil my wooden utensils less often than I probably should [1].

**How I tell a board needs oil:** Freshly oiled wood gets a water-repellent coating, so water beads up on it. Over time water starts soaking in. When big stains develop or the board gets hard to clean, it's time to re-oil [2].

**How I do it:** I use Howard Butcher Block Conditioner and rub it in with a paper towel or an oil rag [2][3].

**When oil isn't enough:** If a board gets really beat up or stained, I sand it with an orbital sander. On one board I also trimmed the sides with a table saw, sanded everything and rechamfered the corners to make it nearly new [3].

questions.question: Would you recommend a cleaver for breaking down the turkey frame? Any specific one?

hybrid.answer:
Yes, I'd recommend a cleaver for breaking down the turkey frame, and the one I'd point you to is the Shibazi Chinese cleaver [1].

**The cleaver:** It's a Chinese-style cleaver from Shibazi. It's online for roughly 40 or 50 bucks, though I can't remember exactly [2]. I use it a lot because it stays sharp, the metal is pretty hard, and it's nice and heavy, so it gets through a turkey carcass pretty easily [2]. It comes in an eight and a nine inch size, and I think mine is the nine [3].

**How I'd use it with shears:** For a bigger turkey, I'd start with heavy-duty shears and cut through as far as I can on each side. Turkeys tend to have one big bone where the wings meet the backbone, and that can be hard to get through [4]. Anywhere the shears struggle, switch to the cleaver [5].

questions.question: When should I salt my steak?

hybrid.answer:
I'd salt it well ahead of cooking: at least 45 minutes before, or even better, the night before, leaving it uncovered in the fridge. [1][2]

**Why ahead of time:** Salt first pulls moisture out, then the brine on the surface breaks down some muscle proteins and gets reabsorbed. Those broken-down proteins tighten up less when cooked, so the steak stays juicier and is seasoned more deeply. [2][3] In my side-by-side, the steak salted overnight had a nicer brown crust and kept its juices, while the unsalted one lost its juices quickly, like wringing out a sponge. [4]

**Uncovered in the fridge:** Leaving it uncovered dries the surface and builds a pellicle, which makes it easier to sear and gives a better browned crust. [1][5] Surface moisture is bad for searing because it takes a lot of energy to evaporate and pulls heat from the pan. [6]

**The minimum:** About 45 minutes is the shortest time I've found for this to work. [2]

**Not too long:** A steak I salted for about 4 days turned ham-like, because the curing breaks the meat down into a smooth texture. [7]

**Preference:** Both ways make a good steak, and which you like is a matter of personal preference. Someone used to unsalted, unrested steak might prefer that texture. [8] If you don't salt ahead, my other option is to sear it straight away. [6]

questions.question: Is the reverse sear still the best way to cook a steak?

hybrid.answer:
Yes. Nearly 20 years after I wrote about it, the reverse sear is still my favorite way to cook a big steak [1]. For a steak this size, it's the way to go [2].

**Why I still like it**
- You get a much more even cook from edge to center, instead of the bullseye pattern from the traditional sear-then-oven method [3].
- The window of perfect doneness is much wider. Traditional cooking can go from 125 to 135 in a couple of minutes, while the reverse sear gives you something like 10, 15 or even 20 minutes before it starts to overcook [4].
- I actually prefer it to sous vide. The oven dries the surface, so the meat sears better, and the fat renders a little better [5].
- No rest is needed, because the temperature is already fairly even all the way through [6].

**Where it works best**
- It works especially well on thick steaks, and it's not really worth it for anything thinner than about an inch and a half [7].

**What has shifted a little**
- For the sear, I used to recommend a sloped sauté pan. These days I prefer a deeper pan like a braiser or Dutch oven, because it contains splatter and sears just as well [8].
- I now also let the salted steak sit for about 45 minutes, or overnight in the fridge, before cooking [9].
- For a fatty cut like a ribeye, I like to go a bit past rare, toward medium-rare to medium, and I aim lower for something lean like a filet [10].

questions.question: Which non-stick pan should I buy?

hybrid.answer:
**Short answer:** I'd go for the Titanium Pro. I co-developed it with Our Place [1], so weigh that when you read my opinion. I use it for virtually all of my non-wok cooking these days [2]. If you mainly want the slickest possible surface, a Teflon-style pan is still the most non-stick, and I keep one for specific jobs like omelets [3].

**Titanium Pro**
- It's not as non-stick as Teflon, but it's better in most other respects [4].
- I can use metal utensils on it, which I can't do with Teflon [5].
- It sears more evenly than Teflon, and I found it my favorite for salmon skin [5].
- Its tall sides aren't ideal for omelets, though it still turned out a good one [6].

**Teflon-style pan**
- It's the slickest option and gives the nicest omelet shape [7].
- I avoid non-stick other than for a few very specific purposes, and I still use it for an omelet [3].
- Coatings scratch and wear, and I retired a five-year-old pan because of that. The coating has a very limited lifespan [8].
- Above around 450°F, these coatings can let off harmful vapors [3]. I wouldn't use Teflon for searing [9].

**Cast iron**
- I'd pick cast iron if I wanted the best possible sear and was willing to put in more time and work [9].

I'd choose based on how you cook. For one non-stick pan that handles most things, I'd get the Titanium Pro. For omelets alone, an inexpensive Teflon-style pan is fine.

questions.question: Is jarred pre-chopped garlic any good?

hybrid.answer:
Mostly no. I'd stay away from jarred pre-chopped garlic, whether it's packed in water or in olive oil, because there's not much flavor left in it [1]. Fresh garlic that you peel yourself is the best [2].

**Why it falls short**
- Once garlic is cut open, its flavor starts to change and you can't really change it back, so any pre-minced or pre-cut garlic has a distinct flavor that differs from natural garlic flavor [3].
- Two of the samples I tasted had a strong citric acid flavor. Citric acid is a preservative used to control water activity and texture, and it completely changes the flavor [4]. I wouldn't recommend those for any raw use [4].
- There was also very little aroma in those samples before cooking [5].

**Where it can work**
- Cooking tames a lot of the sharper, more pungent flavors, so some of the flavor difference evens out, and any of these will sort of work for cooking [4][5].
- If you want a shortcut, pre-peeled cloves are fine for most things, especially cooked [6]. Garlic paste may be an acceptable substitute after that [1].

I'd happily recommend either one, and I currently lean toward the Ooni Koda 16 as my favorite, though the two are close and it comes down to details [1][2].

**Ooni Koda 16:** It fits a bigger pizza, up to 16 inches, which is closer to a real New York style pie [3]. questions.question: Do you ever inject your turkey? And if so, any recommendations on what to use?

hybrid.answer:
I rarely inject my turkey. I have done it in the past, but it's not something I typically do [1]. My main reason is that the injected liquid doesn't get inside the muscle fibers; it mostly sloshes around and separates some of them. The turkey comes out moist, but more the way a sponge is wet than the way a juicy piece of meat is [1].

If you do want to inject, here's what I'd recommend:

- **Well-seasoned stock:** This is one good reason to inject. A stock with salt in it puts the brine inside the turkey, so it brines from the inside as well as the outside, which helps it retain more moisture when you cook and slice it [2].
- **Turkey stock and brown butter:** I've injected a mixture of the two, and I think it can be delicious [2][3].
- **Herb-infused stock or herb butter:** You can infuse turkey stock with a lot of herbs and let it simmer for a bit. Or melt herb butter, combine it with the turkey stock and inject that [3].

I don't generally bother injecting myself, but if you are an injector, those are my recommendations [3].

questions.question: Why do you wash meat before stir-frying?

hybrid.answer:
I wash sliced meat before marinating because it makes a big difference in tenderness. It's a step I never used to do until I started testing it [1].

**Why it works**
- Squeezing and massaging the meat in plenty of cold water pushes out some of the excess juices, which leaves more room for the marinade to penetrate and gives more flavor [2].
- It also loosens up the texture of the muscle, so the meat comes out more tender. Side by side, the difference is stark [2].

**Where I got the idea**
- I picked it up from Wang Gang, a chef from Sichuan who always washes his beef. I then tested it side by side while working on my book [1][2].

**One more theory**
- A chef I corresponded with suggested that in places with hard water, the slightly alkaline makeup of the water may also affect the beef. I only mention this as his idea [2].

**After washing**
- I squeeze the meat out in a fine mesh strainer so the excess water doesn't water down the marinade [3].

I'd also add this washing step to my older beef and broccoli video, since it would improve the texture of the beef [4].

questions.question: Just wondering, what is the best way to clean the wok after each use? And should I use the heat & coat in oil technique after each use as well?

hybrid.answer:
My routine after each use: put the wok on a burner, rinse it out, using soap if you need it, then reheat it on the burner until it's completely dry [1]. I reheat it to get it dry, not for seasoning, because a paper towel or kitchen towel still leaves some moisture behind [1]. With the super nitrided wok you don't have to be as careful about drying as with cast iron, but heating it dry still helps maintain the seasoning [2].

**Stubborn food:** For really burned-on food, heating the wok and then hitting it with water and scrubbing is a great way, and it won't damage the wok [3]. A bamboo wok brush is the best tool for that [3]. It gives good leverage, is inexpensive and is replaceable [4]. I'd skip Bar Keepers Friend on a wok, since it's harsh and would likely strip the black oxide layer [5]. Use a scrubby brush or bamboo brush, plus soap if needed [5]. You don't need to build up or keep thick polymer layers; I wash my wok out until it's smooth every time [5].

**Oil after drying:** Yes, once it's dry I rub in a final thin layer of oil [1]. It matters most if you'll store the wok somewhere with moisture in the air, since an uncoated raw carbon steel wok can rust [6]. If you use it every day or several times a day, it matters less [6]. It's less of an issue with the super nitrided wok because it isn't reactive the way carbon steel is, but with raw carbon steel don't skip it [6]. Warm metal makes the oil easier to rub in and wipe out [7]. Wipe it out as if you'd put it there by accident, because a thick layer can turn gummy and sticky over time [7].

questions.question: A genuine question: if a wok doesn't build up layers of polymers like a cast iron, what does it mean for a wok to build up seasoning?

hybrid.answer:
For a wok, seasoning mostly means the initial conversion of raw carbon steel into black oxide, not building up layers of polymers the way you do in cast iron [1]. Wok seasoning is also more of a per-use thing than a buildup thing [2].

**What seasoning means in a wok**
- With a raw carbon steel wok, the dull silvery gray metal turns black the first time you heat it. That black oxide layer can be considered seasoning [3].
- To get it, I scrub off the machine oil, then heat the wok on every surface until it turns black or bluish black. That's the initial seasoning step [4].
- With induction or electric, I'd blacken at least the bottom, since that's where most cooking happens, or use a blowtorch to reach the rest [5].

**Why polymer layers don't stick around in a wok**
- The bottom gets very hot while the sides stay cooler, so the metal expands unevenly and any hard polymer layer has a hard time staying on [6].
- Stir-frying usually involves deglazing with soy sauce, wine or other acidic liquids, which strip the seasoning [7].
- So I don't expect or aim for a thick polymer layer in a wok, and I advise against deliberately building up carbon [3].

**Per-use routine**
- After cooking, I rinse, dry the wok on the burner, and wipe in a very thin coat of oil to prevent rust without leaving a gummy residue. Before cooking, I rub in a thin layer of oil with a paper towel [8].

**A note on my own wok**
- My super nitrided wok has no coating on it out of the box, so you just rinse it and cook [9].

questions.question: Is there any advantage to salting hours ahead of time with this technique, or does the long time the steak spends hanging out in the oven make that moot? [reverse sear]

hybrid.answer:
Yes, salting ahead still helps with the reverse sear. I salt the steak and let it rest before it goes into the oven, and I don't treat the oven time as a replacement for that.

**Why I still salt ahead**
- Salt first pulls moisture out, then the brine breaks down some muscle proteins and gets reabsorbed. Those proteins tighten less when cooked, so less moisture is squeezed out and the seasoning penetrates better [1].
- About 45 minutes is the minimum for that to happen, so that's what I do before the steak goes into the oven [2].
- In a side-by-side with a pan-seared tenderloin, the steak salted ahead was juicier and more tender [3].

**What changes with the reverse sear**
- Surface moisture matters less, because the steak is going into the oven. The point of the wait is to give the salt time to penetrate [4].
- If you go overnight, uncovered in the fridge, the surface dries and forms a pellicle, so it sears even better. That's optional, and 45 minutes is enough [5].
- I still dry the surface right before searing, since you want it as dry as possible [6].

**What I haven't covered**
I haven't said whether the hours in the low oven could stand in for salting ahead. I always salt first, so I can't speak to that.

questions.question: So, Kenji, since you left Cook's Illustrated, they've started to advocate cold searing (starting in a cold pan and flipping every 2 minutes until done). What are your thoughts?

hybrid.answer:
I haven't covered cold searing, or Cook's Illustrated's current advice on it, in my videos yet.

The closest thing I did cover is my own preferred method for a big steak: the reverse sear. I start the steak in a low oven and finish it with a sear, which gives a much more even cook from edge to center than the traditional method, with its bullseye of doneness [1]. It's still my favorite way to cook a big steak [2].
